THE SPREAD OF PEOPLES · DEEP DIVE

Americas Trade Before 100 CE: Lithic Highways, Old Copper, Olmec Jade & Andean Spondylus

Thousands of years before European ships, Aztec markets, or Inka paved highways, Indigenous Americas communities moved Oregon and Yellowstone volcanic glass over 2,500–4,000 km, mined Lake Superior native copper, imported Pacific *Spondylus* across the Andes, and sailed Guiana nephrite up the Antilles.

Arctic/Bering Strait, Pacific Northwest–Great Basin shell/obsidian, Old Copper & Poverty Point, Hopewell Interaction Sphere, Southwest maize/Gulf shell, Olmec & Preclassic Maya jade/obsidian, Andean *Spondylus*/cacao/cinnabar, and Saladoid–Huecoid Caribbean canoes.

Ice Age and Archaic networks before farming: obsidian, copper and shell

Geochemical sourcing pushes North American long-range conveyance back to Clovis and Early Holocene mobile bands: Knife River flint moved >1,200 km from North Dakota to Colorado, Oregon glass reached Lake Huron and submerged coastal sites, California *Olivella* beads crossed the Sierra into Nevada caves by 7000 BCE, and Labrador Ramah Chert traveled >1,500 km down Atlantic bays. [5] [7] [6]

By 5500–1000 BCE around Lake Superior and at Louisiana's Poverty Point (1700–1100 BCE), fisher-forager communities forged hammered copper tools and hauled metric tons of Arkansas quartz, Missouri galena, Appalachian soapstone, and Gulf shells along Mississippi waterways without maize agriculture. [26] [10] [11] [12]

The Hopewell Interaction Sphere: Rocky Mountains to the Atlantic

Beginning around 200 BCE–100 CE in Ohio's Scioto Valley (Mound City, Hopewell Mound Group) and Illinois River centers, communities assembled the continent's widest pre-contact craft sphere: Obsidian Cliff (Wyoming) and Bear Gulch (Idaho) volcanic glass, Keweenaw native copper breastplates, Ontario Cobalt silver foil panpipes, Blue Ridge mica sheets, grizzly teeth, and Florida *Busycon* whelk shells. [1] [27] [13] [14] [15]

Olmec jadeite, Oaxaca magnetite mirrors and Preclassic Maya obsidian highways

Farther south between 1300 BCE and 100 CE, Gulf Coast Olmec rulers at San Lorenzo and La Venta imported Motagua Valley jadeite celts from Guatemala, concave optical iron-ore mirrors carved in Oaxaca, tons of Isthmian ilmenite cubes, and obsidian from El Chayal, San Martín Jilotepeque, Ixtepeque, and Hidalgo's Pachuca mines. [2] [16] [28] [17] [29]

Meanwhile across Costa Rica's Nicoya peninsula and the Sonoran–Arizona borderlands (bringing domesticated maize and Sea of Cortez *Glycymeris* shells north by 2100–1200 BCE), overlapping agricultural and lapidary networks bridged Middle and North America. [30] [31]

Andean Spondylus, Amazonian cacao, cinnabar and Caribbean canoe lapidaries

Equatorial and South American pre-100 CE trade matched Mesoamerica and Hopewell step-for-step: Upper Amazonian farmers domesticated *Theobroma cacao* at Santa Ana–La Florida (~3300 BCE) alongside Pacific *Spondylus* trade; Caral-Supe and Chavín de Huántar centered warm-water Ecuadorian *Spondylus princeps* and *Strombus* trumpets paired with Ayacucho Quispisisa glass and Huancavelica vermilion cinnabar. [3] [22] [19] [18] [20]

Concurrently in the Lesser Antilles and Puerto Rico (500 BCE–100 CE), Saladoid and Huecoid dugout navigators shipped South American nephrite *muiraquitã* frog amulets, amethyst, and carnelian up island stepping stones to specialized bead-drilling workshops at Trants (Montserrat) and La Hueca (Vieques). [4] [24] [25] [32]
